delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

tools.name: TaskCreate
tools.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

tools.name: TaskGet
tools.description:
Use this tool to retrieve a task by its ID from the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- When you need the full description and context before starting work on a task
- To understand task dependencies (what it blocks, what blocks it)
- After being assigned a task, to get complete requirements

## Output

Returns full task details:
- **subject**: Task title
- **description**: Detailed requirements and context
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **blocks**: Tasks waiting on this one to complete
- **blockedBy**: Tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Tips

- After fetching a task, verify its blockedBy list is empty before beginning work.
- Use TaskList to see all tasks in summary form.

tools.name: TaskList

Use this tool to list all tasks in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- To see what tasks are available to work on (status: 'pending', no owner, not blocked)
- To check overall progress on the project
- To find tasks that are blocked and need dependencies resolved
- After completing a task, to check for newly unblocked work or claim the next available task
- **Prefer working on tasks in ID order** (lowest ID first) when multiple tasks are available, as earlier tasks often set up context for later ones

## Output

Returns a summary of each task:
- **id**: Task identifier (use with TaskGet, TaskUpdate)
- **subject**: Brief description of the task
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **owner**: Agent ID if assigned, empty if available
- **blockedBy**: List of open task IDs that must be resolved first (tasks with blockedBy cannot be claimed until dependencies resolve)

Use TaskGet with a specific task ID to view full details including description and comments.

tools.name: TaskUpdate
tools.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:

    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

toolUseResult.stdout:
The same authorization as `GET /audit` applies, in the same order: a missing, blank or duplicated `X-Audit-Token` gets 401 `unauthorized`, an unknown or expired token 403, and an unreadable or invalid configuration 503 `auth_unavailable` — none of these opens the ledger. `GET /acceptance?key=K` looks up one record; the key stands alone, so combining it with `cursor`, `limit` or `state` is 400 `invalid_request`. Without `key` the query paginates with the exclusive `cursor`, the `limit` page size (1..1000, default 100) and the `state` filter, which only accepts `pending`, `active` or `quarantined`; unknown, repeated or empty parameters and illegal values are 400 `invalid_request` as well. Scope checks follow parameter validation and precede any ledger read: an exact lookup requires unrestricted operation and stage scopes and a key scope that is unrestricted or names the requested key, while a paginated query requires all three scopes unrestricted — anything else is a plain 403.

A successful exact lookup answers 200 with the record object, a successful page with the `{"entries": [[key, record], ...], "next": ...}` object — both in the library's field order, key code-point order, compact UTF-8 and without a trailing newline. Every 200 response carries a strong `ETag`: one double-quoted string of 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, the SHA-256 of the complete response bytes. The exact lookup and the paginated query each tag their own response bytes, so any visible record, order or cursor change changes the tag.

`GET /acceptance` takes an optional `If-None-Match` header: at most one, and only as a single strong tag of that shape. A blank, repeated, weak, wildcard or list conditional is 400 `invalid_request` and never opens the ledger. When the conditional value equals the current snapshot's tag the answer is 304 with an empty body and the same `ETag`; otherwise it is 200 with the full result. The request order is fixed — authorization, query and conditional-header validation, scope checks, and only then the ledger read — and the ledger's shared lock is held from the read through the business-object formation, the response serialization, the digest computation and the conditional comparison, so a request racing a submission decides 200 or 304 from either the complete old ledger or the complete new one, never a mix.

The queries only take the ledger's shared-lock read-only path. A missing ledger gets 404 `acceptance_not_found`, an unknown key 404 `acceptance_key_not_found`, an invalid ledger 409 `acceptance_invalid`, and other read failures 503 `acceptance_unavailable`; real paths and system messages never appear in an error.

## Migration batch queries

```bash
python -m carbon_market serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --audit PATH --auth CONFIG --migration-batches COORD
```

`--migration-batches` exposes the one fixed migration-batch coordination ledger at `COORD` as read-only `GET /migration-batches`; it may only be given together with `--audit` and the multi-token `--auth` method — alone, empty, repeated, without `--audit` or paired with the single `--token` it is a usage error (exit status 2) and nothing listens. The client can neither pass nor probe any other file path: the ledger is fixed at startup. Without it the path stays a plain 404 like any other unknown path, and every other interface is unchanged.

Authorization is the existing audit authorization and the request order is fixed — identity, query parameters, scope, and only then the ledger read; a failure at one stage never opens a later stage's files. A missing, blank or duplicated `X-Audit-Token` gets 401 `unauthorized`, an unknown or expired token 403 `forbidden`, and an unreadable or invalid configuration 503 `auth_unavailable`. Unknown, repeated or empty parameters and illegal combinations get 400 `invalid_request`. `GET /migration-batches?key=K` returns only that batch's snapshot; the key stands alone, so `cursor` or `limit` beside it is 400, and an unknown batch is a distinct 404 `migration_batch_not_found`. Without `key` the query paginates in ascending batch-key code-point order with an exclusive `cursor` and a `limit` page size (a decimal integer from 1 to 1000, default 100). The page object has, in order, `entries` and `next`; each entry carries, in order, the batch `key`, the complete batch `snapshot` and `completion`. An active batch's `completion` is `null`; a terminal batch's completion is `{"index": i, "at": t}` — the batch's zero-based position in the coordination audit (the real completion order) and its completion moment — so the public completion order and per-item errors are observable. `next` is the key of the page's last entry when more batches remain, else `null`.

Scope checks follow parameter validation and precede every file read, using the same records as `GET /audit`: an exact lookup requires unrestricted operation and stage scopes and a key scope that is unrestricted or names the requested batch, while a paginated query requires the operation, stage and history-key scopes all unrestricted — anything else is a plain 403.

The coordination ledger's shared lock together with the nine business ledgers' shared locks covers the ledger reads, the page/snapshot formation and the response serialization, so a concurrent batch writer is observed as either the complete old or the complete new version, never a mix; responses are compact UTF-8 JSON with no trailing newline. Before any lock or business ledger is touched, an existing coordination file must first prove its own format — UTF-8, JSON (no negative-zero or non-finite literals), version 1, the fixed field sets and key order and the exact canonical bytes; any such violation raises even when the requested key is absent and is never masked by it. The read never creates the coordination file, a lock file, a directory or any other trace: a miss is decided by an unlocked read before a companion lock file is opened. A missing coordination ledger gets 404 `migration_batches_not_found`; non-canonical content, a broken cross-reference or a referenced business ledger that is missing gets 409 `migration_batches_invalid`; any other read failure gets 503 `migration_batches_unavailable`. Error bodies contain only `error` and never leak a path or system message.

The library surface is `migration_batch.get(ledger, key)` (one snapshot, `KeyError` for a missing ledger or unknown key), `migration_batch.search(ledger, cursor=None, limit=100)` (the page object), and the lock-holding `get_response`/`search_response` serializers the endpoint serves.

## Resource supply and feasibility

The `carbon_market.resources` module complements job acceptance with a persistent, versioned resource-supply registry and a feasibility query over it. `resources.publish(path, resource, idempotency_key)` publishes one supply version: the resource object carries exactly `resource_id`, `region`, `capacity`, `start`, `end`, `unit_cost`, `carbon_intensity` and `residency` — non-empty id and region strings, a positive integer capacity, non-boolean non-negative start, end, unit cost and carbon intensity with start not later than end, and a residency list of distinct non-empty strings sorted by code point that contains the resource's own region. A first publication returns the canonical record — the resource fields plus the next consecutive `version` for that resource id — with `True`, and atomically commits the record, the idempotency binding and a publish audit event binding key, resource id and version. Replaying the same key with an identical resource returns the stored record with `False` and writes nothing; the same key with a different resource, or a new version whose start does not strictly increase over the resource's current latest, raises `ValueError`.

`resources.get(path, resource_id, version=None)` reads one record back: the latest version when `version` is omitted, otherwise the exact version. An unknown resource id or version raises `KeyError`.

`resources.feasible(job_path, supply_path, job_id, at)` joins a `jobs.submit` acceptance file with the supply file — both read as complete snapshots while their shared locks are held together — and ranks the resources that can serve job `job_id` at the non-boolean non-negative evaluation moment `at`. Each resource contributes only its highest version valid at `at`; a candidate must sit in one of the job's regions, offer at least the job's work as capacity, cover the job's residency regions, and stay available at least until the job's deadline. The total cost is the job's work times the unit cost and the total carbon the work times the carbon intensity; exceeding either budget excludes the candidate. The result is ordered by carbon intensity, then unit cost, then resource id, each entry carrying the resource record and both totals — an empty list when nothing qualifies. A version-1 `jobs.register` file is invalid structure here, and an unknown job id raises `KeyError`.

The supply file is one compact UTF-8 JSON document — version, history sorted by resource id and version, idempotency map sorted by key, audit events — with non-ASCII written through and exactly one trailing newline; negative-zero and non-finite number literals are illegal. Every read entry (`publish`, `get` and `feasible`, and any consumer of the supply file) requires the on-disk bytes to be exactly that canonical form: a file whose fields or keys are out of order, which carries any whitespace beyond the structural tokens, which escapes non-ASCII characters, or which misses or doubles the final newline is rejected with `ValueError` just like a malformed or structurally invalid file. Publishing commits under the per-real-path cross-process exclusive lock with pre-call byte restoration on commit failure, queries take the shared lock, and invalid arguments, values, encodings, JSON, structure, ordering, canonical bytes or references raise `ValueError`, missing input files or publish parent directories `FileNotFoundError`, and other locking or I/O failures `OSError`.

## Market clearing

The `carbon_market.market.clear(jobs, supply, ledger, job_id, key, at)` entry adds the new-market clearing ledger on top of accepted jobs and the versioned resource supply. The three paths, `job_id` and `key` must be non-empty strings, `at` a non-boolean non-negative integer evaluation moment, and the three paths must resolve to distinct real locations; any violation raises `ValueError` before any business file is read.

The acceptance file and the supply file are read as one snapshot under their shared locks, together with the ledger's exclusive lock; the three locks are taken in resolved real-path sorted order so concurrent calls can never deadlock. Only each resource's highest version valid at `at` is considered, and region, residency, cost budget, carbon budget, deadline coverage and the candidate entries (`resource`, `total_cost`, `total_carbon`) follow exactly the `resources.feasible` semantics. In addition, each resource version's capacity is reduced by the work of every trade already booked against that exact resource version in the ledger, so concurrent clearings can never oversell capacity and bookings never cross resource versions. The remaining candidates are ordered by carbon intensity, unit cost and resource id; the first one is the unique winner.

The call returns `(trade, created)`. The trade binds the job id, the evaluation moment, the work, the complete ordered candidate snapshot and a versioned selection (`resource_id`, `version`). A missing ledger is created only when the first trade is made; the trade, the idempotency binding (key to job id and evaluation moment) and the audit event binding the request key, the resource id and its selected version are committed together — ledger sections sorted by code point, compact UTF-8 JSON with non-ASCII written through and one trailing newline, written through a synced same-directory temporary file, atomic replace and directory fsync; a failed commit restores the pre-call bytes (or removes a ledger that did not exist).

Replaying the same key with the same job and evaluation moment returns the stored trade with `False` without reselecting a resource, appending an event or rewriting a byte. The same key with a changed request, or a job already traded under another idempotency key, raises `ValueError` and leaves the ledger byte-for-byte untouched. An unknown job raises `KeyError` and no remaining feasible resource raises `LookupError`; neither creates the ledger. Missing input files or a missing ledger parent raise `FileNotFoundError` without leaving a ledger or temporary fragment. Invalid ledger structure, references, ordering or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`; other locking, read/write or sync failures raise `OSError`. The existing `market.match`, the `resources` interfaces, serving and HTTP behavior are unchanged.

## Dispatch commitments

The `carbon_market.dispatch` module adds the scheduling-commitment layer on top of the clearing ledger, with four persistent, idempotent calls over one dispatch ledger (`version`, `decisions` sorted by job id, `idempotency` and `audit` sorted by key — compact UTF-8 JSON with non-ASCII written through, no negative-zero or non-finite literals, exactly one trailing newline).

`dispatch.commit(jobs, supply, trades, ledger, job_id, key, at)` reads the acceptance file, the supply file and the clearing ledger as one snapshot under their shared locks together with the dispatch ledger's exclusive lock, all four taken in resolved real-path order, and creates the job's decision: it binds the traded resource id and version and the job's deadline, and starts `ready` with zero attempts and no owner or lease. The dispatch ledger is created only by this first commit. An unknown job raises `KeyError`, a job without a recorded trade `LookupError`, and a commit moment past the job's deadline `TimeoutError`.

`dispatch.claim(ledger, job_id, key, owner, lease, at)` moves a `ready` or `failed` decision to `claimed` under a non-empty owner with a positive integer lease, counting one more attempt; the lease ends at `at + lease` and may not pass the job's deadline. A decision still held under a valid lease, or a lease end beyond the deadline, raises `TimeoutError`. `dispatch.finish(ledger, job_id, key, owner, result, at)` lets the current owner inside its lease record `succeeded` or `failed` and clears owner and lease; a non-claimed decision or an illegal result raises `ValueError`, a different owner `PermissionError`, and a moment past the lease end `TimeoutError`. `dispatch.recover(ledger, job_id, key, at)` returns a decision whose lease has strictly expired to `ready` without counting an attempt; recovering before strict expiry raises `PermissionError`. These three actions take only the dispatch ledger's exclusive lock and fail with `FileNotFoundError` when the ledger does not exist.

All four calls return `(decision, created)`; replaying a key with an equivalent request returns the current decision with `False` and writes nothing, while the same key with a different action, job, owner, result, moment or lease raises `ValueError`. Every first-served key commits the decision, the idempotency binding (the complete request) and the audit event (request plus committed decision snapshot) in one synced atomic write that restores the pre-call bytes on failure, so no failed call leaves a half-state. Invalid arguments, nulls, types, structure, ordering, references or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`, missing inputs or parents `FileNotFoundError`, and other locking or I/O failures `OSError`. The existing `market.clear`, the `resources` interfaces, the reservation migration, serving and HTTP behavior are unchanged.

## Execution plans

The `carbon_market.execution` module adds the recoverable execution layer on top of the dispatch ledger, with three persistent, idempotent calls over one execution ledger (`version`, `plans` keyed by job id and dispatch attempt, `idempotency` and `audit` sorted by key — compact UTF-8 JSON with non-ASCII written through, no negative-zero or non-finite literals, exactly one trailing newline).

`execution.plan(jobs, supply, trades, dispatch, ledger, job_id, key, owner, source, at)` reads the acceptance file, the supply file, the clearing ledger and the dispatch ledger as one snapshot under their shared locks together with the execution ledger's exclusive lock, all five taken in resolved real-path order, and creates the plan for one `claimed` decision held by `owner` and still inside its lease — a decision in any other state raises `ValueError`, a different owner `PermissionError`, a moment past the lease end `TimeoutError`. The plan is numbered by the decision's dispatch attempt count and fixes the job, the traded resource id and version, the deadline, the owner and the lease end; one dispatch attempt yields at most one plan. An empty `source` (`None` or `""`) creates a `launch` plan whose steps are `stage` then `start`; a non-empty `source` creates a `migrate` plan whose steps are `copy` then `switch`, and the source must name a published resource other than the target whose residency list covers the job's residency regions, else `LookupError`. A job without a recorded trade raises `LookupError` as well, and an unknown job or decision `KeyError`. The execution ledger is created only by this first plan.

`execution.record(ledger, job_id, attempt, key, owner, step, result, receipt, at)` appends one step receipt — the step, `succeeded` or `failed`, a non-empty receipt string and the moment — to an active plan; steps advance only on success, a receipt naming anything but the next pending step raises `ValueError`, a failed step terminates the plan as `failed`, a successful last step as `completed`, and terminal plans accept no further receipts. Only the plan's owner acting inside the lease may record: a different owner raises `PermissionError` and a moment past the lease end `TimeoutError`. `execution.recover(ledger, job_id, attempt, key, at)` turns an active plan whose lease has strictly expired `interrupted`, preserving every recorded receipt; recovering before strict expiry raises `PermissionError`. These two calls take only the execution ledger's exclusive lock and fail with `FileNotFoundError` when the ledger does not exist.

All three calls return `(plan, created)` and share one idempotency key space; replaying a key with an equivalent request returns the current plan with `False` and writes nothing, while the same key with a different action, job, attempt, owner, source, step, result, receipt or moment raises `ValueError`. Every first-served key commits the plan, the idempotency binding (the complete request) and the audit event (request plus committed plan snapshot) in one synced atomic write that restores the pre-call bytes on failure. An unknown job or attempt raises `KeyError`; invalid arguments, nulls, types, structure, ordering, references or non-canonical bytes raise `ValueError`, missing inputs or parents `FileNotFoundError`, and other locking or I/O failures `OSError`. The existing `dispatch` interfaces, `market.clear`, the `resources` interfaces, serving and HTTP behavior are unchanged.

## Execution synchronization

The `carbon_market.execution_sync` module adds the persistent reconciliation layer on top of the execution and dispatch ledgers with one call, `execution_sync.run(execution, dispatch, ledger, owner, key, now, lease)`. The three ledger paths must be non-empty strings resolving to distinct real locations, `owner` and `key` non-empty strings, `now` a non-boolean non-negative integer moment and `lease` a non-boolean positive integer coordination lease; any violation raises `ValueError` before a business file is read.

The first call for a batch `key` scans the execution ledger by job id and attempt and fixes the batch as exactly the terminal plans (`completed`, `failed` or `interrupted`) no earlier batch has already synced. A `completed` plan finishes the dispatch decision as succeeded, a `failed` plan as failed, and an `interrupted` plan recovers the strictly expired claim; the action moment is always history — the last step receipt's moment for a finish, the recorded execution-recovery moment for a recover — and a retry can never rewrite it. Each item is first persisted `pending` in the coordination ledger, and only then is the existing `dispatch.finish`/`dispatch.recover` interface called with an idempotency key derived stably from the batch key and the plan identity, so a crash re-entry replays the very same request. The item becomes `applied` only after a successful call or an equivalent replay, saving the returned decision; a failure records the public exception class, keeps the item pending and re-raises the original exception with its chain.

The call returns `(batch, created)`, a fixed-order copy of the current batch snapshot and the first-creation flag. The same batch key fixes its first scan forever: re-entry continues the unfinished items and a completed batch replays without rewriting a byte; terminal plans appearing later require a new batch key, and even an empty first scan commits an explicit `completed` state with the full audit snapshot. An active batch may only be continued by its current owner — a different owner before strict lease expiry raises `PermissionError` — while after expiry another owner may take over without repeating any applied item. Before any advance, the dispatch decision's state, attempt, owner and lease are checked against the plan (as is a dispatch idempotency key already bound to a different request); any mismatch raises `ValueError` without advancing.

The coordination ledger (`version`, `batches` sorted by key with each batch's items sorted, and an append-only `audit`) is one compact UTF-8 JSON document with non-ASCII written through, decimal integers and exactly one trailing newline. The nine paths are the eight lifecycle paths plus the settlement ledger; they, `job_id`, `plan_key` and `key` must be non-empty strings resolving to distinct real locations and `at` a non-boolean non-negative integer settlement moment, all checked before a business file is read. `plan_key` is the idempotency key of the `start` request that created the plan. The eight inputs are read as one snapshot under shared locks and the settlement ledger under its exclusive lock, all nine taken in resolved real-path order.
232:Only a terminal plan settles. An `active` plan raises `PermissionError` and creates no record; a missing job, intent or plan, or a `plan_key` that is not the plan's start key, raises `KeyError`. A settlement moment earlier than the terminal evidence — the last step receipt, or the recorded recovery moment for an `interrupted` plan — raises `ValueError`; a legitimate late recovery whose settlement runs past the job deadline is still accepted, so no deadline timeout is enforced. Contradictory terminal evidence, the same key carrying a changed request, another key settling the same migration, a broken running generation or contradictory snapshot references raise `ValueError`.
234:A `migrated` plan confirms the target version as the current occupancy (`active`) and records the source version as the previous-generation binding; a `failed` or `interrupted` plan forms a compensation (`compensated`): the current occupancy stays on the source version and the target reservation stays released. The record freezes, in order, `job_id`, `plan_key`, the continuous running `generation` (the immutable trade is generation 0, the settlement generation 1), the source terminal state `migration`, the `before` and `after` resource selections (`resource_id`/`version`), the settlement moment `at`, the `state` (`pending`, `active`, `compensated`) and `audit` — the sorted, deduplicated idempotency keys of every intent-ledger action the migration committed (reservation, claim, step receipts and recovery).

The queries only take the ledger's shared-lock read-only path. A missing ledger gets 404 `acceptance_not_found`, an unknown key 404 `acceptance_key_not_found`, an invalid ledger 409 `acceptance_invalid`, and other read failures 503 `acceptance_unavailable`; real paths and system messages never appear in an error.

## Migration batch queries

```bash
python -m carbon_market serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --audit PATH --auth CONFIG --migration-batches COORD
```

`--migration-batches` exposes the one fixed migration-batch coordination ledger at `COORD` as read-only `GET /migration-batches`; it may only be given together with `--audit` and the multi-token `--auth` method — alone, empty, repeated, without `--audit` or paired with the single `--token` it is a usage error (exit status 2) and nothing listens. The client can neither pass nor probe any other file path: the ledger is fixed at startup. Without it the path stays a plain 404 like any other unknown path, and every other interface is unchanged.

Authorization is the existing audit authorization and the request order is fixed — identity, query parameters, scope, and only then the ledger read; a failure at one stage never opens a later stage's files. A missing, blank or duplicated `X-Audit-Token` gets 401 `unauthorized`, an unknown or expired token 403 `forbidden`, and an unreadable or invalid configuration 503 `auth_unavailable`. Unknown, repeated or empty parameters and illegal combinations get 400 `invalid_request`. `GET /migration-batches?key=K` returns only that batch's snapshot; the key stands alone, so `cursor` or `limit` beside it is 400, and an unknown batch is a distinct 404 `migration_batch_not_found`. Without `key` the query paginates in ascending batch-key code-point order with an exclusive `cursor` and a `limit` page size (a decimal integer from 1 to 1000, default 100). The page object has, in order, `entries` and `next`; each entry carries, in order, the batch `key`, the complete batch `snapshot` and `completion`. An active batch's `completion` is `null`; a terminal batch's completion is `{"index": i, "at": t}` — the batch's zero-based position in the coordination audit (the real completion order) and its completion moment — so the public completion order and per-item errors are observable. `next` is the key of the page's last entry when more batches remain, else `null`.

Scope checks follow parameter validation and precede every file read, using the same records as `GET /audit`: an exact lookup requires unrestricted operation and stage scopes and a key scope that is unrestricted or names the requested batch, while a paginated query requires the operation, stage and history-key scopes all unrestricted — anything else is a plain 403.

The coordination ledger's shared lock together with the nine business ledgers' shared locks covers the ledger reads, the page/snapshot formation and the response serialization, so a concurrent batch writer is observed as either the complete old or the complete new version, never a mix; responses are compact UTF-8 JSON with no trailing newline. Before any lock or business ledger is touched, an existing coordination file must first prove its own format — UTF-8, JSON (no negative-zero or non-finite literals), version 1, the fixed field sets and key order and the exact canonical bytes; any such violation raises even when the requested key is absent and is never masked by it. The read never creates the coordination file, a lock file, a directory or any other trace: a miss is decided by an unlocked read before a companion lock file is opened. A missing coordination ledger gets 404 `migration_batches_not_found`; non-canonical content, a broken cross-reference or a referenced business ledger that is missing gets 409 `migration_batches_invalid`; any other read failure gets 503 `migration_batches_unavailable`. Error bodies contain only `error` and never leak a path or system message.

The library surface is `migration_batch.get(ledger, key)` (one snapshot, `KeyError` for a missing ledger or unknown key), `migration_batch.search(ledger, cursor=None, limit=100)` (the page object), and the lock-holding `get_response`/`search_response` serializers the endpoint serves.

1	"""Persistent cross-job migration batches.
2	
3	The single-job layers already cover one booking end to end -- the trade,
4	dispatch, a launch plan, a migration advice with its reservation, claim,
5	receipts, recovery and a terminal settlement fixing the job's current
6	binding -- but nothing coordinates those steps across jobs. This module
7	adds the coordination: one persistent migration batch takes one complete
8	snapshot of the nine business ledgers, fixes its members, drives each
9	member's ``keep``/``migrate`` round with optional per-job receipts,
10	survives a crash mid-batch and settles every terminal migration before
11	the batch closes.
12	
13	:func:`run` is the only write entry point. The first call for a batch
14	key fixes the members forever: every accepted job that already holds a
15	trade and is not driven by another still-open batch, ordered by job id.
16	The judgment is rooted at the latest completed binding
17	``rebalance.current`` returns (the immutable trade when there is none):
18	
19	* a job with no current-round migration evidence whose booking is
20	  finished or in flight through the baseline layers simply stays on its
21	  current binding (``keep``);
22	* otherwise a fresh advice is evaluated at the batch moment; a ``keep``
23	  advice completes directly and a ``migrate`` advice is reserved and
24	  claimed under stable request keys;
25	* an unclaimed reservation rooted at the current binding is claimed;
26	* an active plan receives the receipt that names its next pending step,
27	  waits while the plan lease is valid without such a receipt, and is
28	  recovered once the lease has strictly expired;
29	* a ``migrated``, ``failed`` or ``interrupted`` plan rooted at the
30	  current binding enters settlement.
31	
32	Every downstream action (``evaluate``, ``apply``, ``start``, ``record``,
33	``recover``, ``settle``) and its full parameters are persisted under a
34	stable request key *before* the existing interface is called, and the
35	item only advances after success, so a crashed call replays the very
36	same request and a completed phase is never redone; a persisted request
37	always belongs to the generation it rooted and receipts, recovery and
38	settlement name that plan explicitly, never a later generation. One
39	member's business exception saves the public exception class and fails
40	just that member, while the other members continue.
41	
42	An active batch may only be continued by its current owner; another
43	owner may take over only after the coordination lease has strictly
44	expired. A member that drives a migration plan keeps the plan's actual
45	step receipts -- the credential text verbatim, including non-ASCII -- in
46	its most recent snapshot, never just a stage marker. A receipt that is
47	fully equivalent to a step already saved returns the current progress
48	instead of failing the member, while any change to that step's result,
49	credential or moment raises ``ValueError`` with the coordination bytes
50	untouched; if the step previously landed downstream but the coordination
51	snapshot has not advanced yet, re-entry catches the original action up
52	exactly once.
53	
54	The coordination ledger (version 1, sections ``version``, key-sorted
55	``batches`` and an append-only ``audit``) is one compact UTF-8 JSON
56	document with non-ASCII written through, decimal integers and exactly
57	one trailing newline. The audit is appended in the real order batches
58	complete and is never re-sorted by batch key; each completed batch has
59	exactly one event whose snapshot equals that batch's complete state at
60	completion. Ledgers written without the per-item receipts field still
61	load and replay byte-for-byte; a batch a run rewrites gains that field.
62	"""

255	def _plan_key_for(batch_key: str, job_id: str) -> str:
256	    # The migration plan's own start key for a plan this batch begins;
257	    # it binds every later receipt, recovery and settlement to this one
258	    # generation so a pending request can never cross into a later plan.
259	    return _stable_key(batch_key, job_id, "start")

262	def _settle_key_for(plan_key: str) -> str:
263	    # The settlement key derives from the plan's start key alone, so a
264	    # crash between settle's pending and final writes is replayed under
265	    # the same key even by a later batch that picks the plan up.
266	    return f"{len(plan_key)}:settle\t{plan_key}"

277	    def __init__(self, reals: dict[str, str]) -> None:
278	        self.reals = reals
279	        # The seven baseline layers are read exactly as
280	        # rebalance._load_snapshot_layers does, except that a missing
281	        # advice ledger is an empty one: the first member that judges a
282	        # round creates it through rebalance.evaluate.
283	        accepted, _job_map, _job_events, job_raw = \
284	            _rebalance._jobs._load_submit_file(reals["jobs"])
285	        if job_raw is None:
286	            raise FileNotFoundError(
287	                f"acceptance file {reals['jobs']!r} does not exist")
288	        if job_raw != _rebalance._jobs._serialize_submit_file(
289	                accepted, _job_map, _job_events):
290	            raise ValueError(
291	                f"acceptance file {reals['jobs']!r} is not in canonical "
292	                "compact form")
293	        history, _supply_map, _supply_events, supply_raw = \
294	            _rebalance._resources._load_file(reals["supply"])
295	        if supply_raw is None:
296	            raise FileNotFoundError(
297	                f"supply file {reals['supply']!r} does not exist")
298	        signal_history, _signal_map, _signal_events, signal_raw = \
299	            _rebalance._signals._load_file(reals["signals"])
300	        if signal_raw is None:
301	            raise FileNotFoundError(
302	                f"signal file {reals['signals']!r} does not exist")
303	        cleared, _clear_keys, trades_raw = _rebalance._market.\
304	            _load_clear_ledger(
305	                reals["trades"], accepted, history, signal_history)
306	        if trades_raw is None:
307	            raise FileNotFoundError(
308	                f"clearing ledger {reals['trades']!r} does not exist")
309	        decisions, _dispatch_keys, _dispatch_events, dispatch_raw = \
310	            _rebalance._dispatch._load_ledger(reals["dispatch"])
311	        if dispatch_raw is None:
312	            raise FileNotFoundError(
313	                f"dispatch ledger {reals['dispatch']!r} does not exist")
314	        self.exec_plans, _plan_keys, _plan_events = \
315	            _rebalance._execution._load_existing_ledger(
316	                reals["execution"])[:3]
317	        advice_records, _advice_events, _advice_raw = \
318	            _rebalance._load_ledger(
319	                reals["advice"], accepted, cleared, history,
320	                signal_history, defer_current=True)
321	        self.accepted = accepted
322	        self.history = history
323	        self.signal_history = signal_history
324	        self.cleared = cleared
325	        self.decisions = decisions
326	        self.advice_records = advice_records
327	        intents, plans, idempotency, events, version, intent_raw = \
328	            _rebalance._load_intent_ledger(
329	                reals["ledger"], self.accepted, self.cleared, self.history,
330	                self.signal_history, self.advice_records)
331	        if intent_raw is not None \
332	                and version != _rebalance._INTENT_VERSION_V3:
333	            # Only the history layout keeps every generation apart; a
334	            # legacy ledger is upgraded in memory for reading and is
335	            # never rewritten by this module. A missing ledger is simply
336	            # empty: the first downstream apply creates it.
337	            intents, plans, idempotency, events = \
338	                _rebalance._upgrade_intent_ledger_v3(
339	                    intents, plans, idempotency, events)
340	        self.intents = intents
341	        self.plans = plans
342	        self.idempotency = idempotency
343	        self.events = events
344	        records, settle_bindings, _events, _settle_raw = _rebalance.\
345	            _load_settlement_ledger(
346	                reals["settlements"], self.accepted, self.cleared, plans,
347	                idempotency, events, _rebalance._INTENT_VERSION_V3)
348	        # A missing settlement ledger is simply empty: the first member
349	        # that reaches settlement creates it through rebalance.settle.
350	        self.settlements = records
351	        self.settle_bindings = settle_bindings
352	        self.completed, self.pending_jobs = \
353	            _rebalance._lineage_from_settlement_records(records)
354	        for advice_record in self.advice_records.values():
355	            _rebalance._ground_advice_current(
356	                advice_record, self.cleared,
357	                _rebalance._settlement_currents(self.completed))

367	    def current_binding(self, job_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
368	        # The judgment source is current: the latest completed binding
369	        # or the immutable trade's frozen version as generation 0.
370	        latest = _rebalance._latest_completed_binding(
371	            self.completed, job_id)
372	        if latest is not None:
373	            return copy.deepcopy(latest["after"])
374	        trade = self.cleared[job_id]

378	    def rooted_plans(self, job_id: str,
379	                     binding: dict[str, Any]) -> list[tuple[str,
380	                                                            dict[str, Any]]]:
381	        return sorted(((start_key, plan) for start_key, plan
382	                       in self.plans.items()
383	                       if plan["job_id"] == job_id
384	                       and plan["source"] == binding),
385	                      key=lambda entry: (entry[1]["at"], entry[0]))
386	
387	    def unclaimed_rooted_intent(
388	        self, job_id: str, binding: dict[str, Any],
389	    ) -> tuple[str, dict[str, Any]] | None:
390	        # The newest reservation rooted at the current binding that no
391	        # start request has claimed yet.
392	        claimed = _rebalance._claimed_intent_refs(
393	            self.plans, self.idempotency, _rebalance._INTENT_VERSION_V3)
394	        candidates = [(ref, intent) for ref, intent in self.intents.items()
395	                      if ref not in claimed and intent["job_id"] == job_id
396	                      and intent["source"] == binding]
397	        if not candidates:
398	            return None
399	        return max(candidates, key=lambda entry: (entry[1]["at"], entry[0]))

401	    def terminal_moment(self, plan: dict[str, Any],
402	                        plan_key: str) -> int:
403	        return _rebalance._terminal_plan_at(
404	            plan, self.events, plan_key, _rebalance._INTENT_VERSION_V3)

406	    def settle_request(
407	        self, job_id: str, plan_key: str, at: int, fallback_key: str,
408	    ) -> tuple[str, int]:
409	        # When a previous crashed run already bound a settlement request
410	        # to this terminal plan, re-entry (even from a later batch)
411	        # replays that same key and moment; otherwise the caller's
412	        # stable key is used for the first settlement.
413	        for existing_key, request in self.settle_bindings.items():
414	            if request["job_id"] == job_id \
415	                    and request["plan_key"] == plan_key:
416	                return existing_key, request["at"]
417	        return fallback_key, at

425	_MARKER_REQUEST_FIELDS = {
426	    "evaluate": ("at",),
427	    "apply": ("advice_key", "at"),
428	    "start": ("owner", "lease_end", "at"),
429	    "record": ("owner", "step", "result", "receipt", "at"),
430	    "recover": ("owner", "at"),
431	    "settle": ("plan_key", "at"),
432	}

434	
435	def _marker(action: str, **params: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
436	    # Persisted before the downstream interface is called: the action
437	    # name and the exact parameters the crash re-entry must replay.
438	    return {"action": action,
439	            "request": {field: params[field]
440	                        for field in _MARKER_REQUEST_FIELDS[action]}}
441	
442	
443	def _is_marker(value: object) -> bool:
444	    return isinstance(value, dict) \
445	        and set(value.keys()) == {"action", "request"} \
446	        and isinstance(value.get("action"), str) \
447	        and isinstance(value.get("request"), dict)
